title: 22. Interview: Knowledge Graphs
summary: Interview Q&A for Knowledge Graphs — 5 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 5 Knowledge Graphs interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 11 — Interview Preparation
sections.body:
### A. Conceptual Interview Questions

**Q1: What is a knowledge graph triple and why is the triple store model powerful?**
> **Answer:** A triple is (Subject, Predicate, Object) — the minimal unit of factual representation. Example: (Apple, IS_CEO_OF, Tim Cook). The power: any complex real-world knowledge can be decomposed into triples. A set of triples forms a directed graph where subjects and objects are nodes, predicates are edges. This enables: (1) flexible schema evolution — add new fact types by adding new predicates, (2) natural query as graph traversal — follow predicate chains, (3) integration — triples from multiple sources can be merged on shared subjects, (4) reasoning — infer new facts from chains of triples (if A ACQUIRED B and B HAS_CEO C, then A likely controls C's career).

**Q2: How does Cypher's MERGE differ from CREATE?**
> **Answer:** CREATE always creates a new node/relationship — will create duplicates. MERGE: creates only if the pattern doesn't exist, otherwise matches and optionally updates. Crucial for idempotent graph loading. Example: `MERGE (n:Person {canonical_id: $id}) ON CREATE SET n.name = $name ON MATCH SET n.mention_count = coalesce(n.mention_count, 0) + 1`. This safely handles concurrent document processing where multiple jobs might try to create the same entity. MERGE with a unique constraint = exactly-once semantics for node creation.

**Q3: What is the Leiden community detection algorithm and why is it used in GraphRAG?**
> **Answer:** Leiden is an improved version of the Louvain algorithm for community detection in graphs. It identifies hierarchical clusters of tightly interconnected nodes. In Microsoft GraphRAG: after building the knowledge graph, Leiden groups related entities into communities (e.g., "Apple ecosystem", "Google ecosystem"). Each community is then summarized by an LLM into a "community report" — a natural language summary of that cluster's main concepts and relationships. For global queries ("What are the main themes?"), GraphRAG retrieves relevant community reports and synthesizes them, instead of traversing individual entities. This makes it possible to answer broad questions about large graphs without traversing millions of nodes.

**Q4: How would you handle the graph explosion problem in practice?**
> **Answer:** Multiple techniques in combination: (1) Relationship type filtering — only traverse relevant edge types for the query (medical queries: TREATS, CAUSES; not LOCATED_IN). (2) Hop depth limiting — max 2-3 hops for most queries; deeper = exponential growth. (3) Beam search — at each hop, keep only top-K nodes by relevance score, discard the rest. (4) Hub node detection — entities with degree > 1000 are flagged; apply stricter filtering when traversing from/through them. (5) Node limit circuit breaker — if traversal exceeds N nodes, stop and return what you have. (6) Caching — pre-compute and cache traversals for top-1000 queried entities. (7) Query planning — estimate traversal cost before executing, fall back to vector search for high-cost queries.

**Q5: What are graph embeddings and how do they extend knowledge graph capabilities?**
> **Answer:** Graph embeddings (Node2Vec, TransE, ComplEx) learn vector representations for nodes and relationships such that graph structure is captured in the vector space. Node2Vec: random walks on graph → Word2Vec on walk sequences → nodes that co-appear in walks get similar vectors. TransE: learn embeddings such that h + r ≈ t for each triple (head + relation ≈ tail). Applications in GraphRAG: (1) Entity similarity without direct relationship — "Apple" and "Samsung" are similar in graph because both connect to "phone", "Android/iOS", "consumer electronics". (2) Link prediction — which new relationships are likely based on embedding geometry. (3) Hybrid retrieval — use node embeddings for ANN search, then traverse graph for context.

### B. Scenario Questions

**Scenario: Knowledge graph query returns 0 results for "Tell me about CRISPR applications in gene therapy"**

> **Step-by-step investigation:**
> 1. Check if "CRISPR" entity exists in graph: `MATCH (n {name: 'CRISPR'}) RETURN n` → if 0 → entity not extracted
> 2. Search variations: "CRISPR-Cas9", "CRISPR/Cas9", "clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats"
> 3. Check entity linker: is "CRISPR" linked to the wrong canonical entity?
> 4. If entity exists: check degree — does it have relationships? → If degree=0, relationship extraction failed
> 5. Check traversal: is "gene therapy" a concept in graph connected to CRISPR?
>
> **Likely root causes:**
> - Generic NER missed "CRISPR" as entity (biotechnology-specific term)
> - Entity resolution failed: "CRISPR" ≠ "CRISPR-Cas9" in graph
> - Relationship extraction missed "CRISPR USED_IN gene therapy"
>
> **Fix:** Domain-specific NER for biotech, synonym expansion in entity linker

### D. System Design Question

**Design: Legal knowledge graph for a law firm with 50 years of case law**

```
SCALE:
  - 2M court decisions
  - 500K statutes and regulations  
  - 100K legal entities (firms, judges, parties)
  
GRAPH SCHEMA:
  Nodes:
    - Case (docket, court, date, outcome)
    - Statute (code, section, jurisdiction)
    - LegalConcept (precedent, doctrine)
    - Entity (firm, person, organization)
    - Judge (name, court, appointee)
  
  Relationships:
    - CITES (case → case, statute)
    - AFFIRMED_BY, OVERRULED_BY (case → case)
    - INTERPRETED_BY (statute → case)
    - APPLIES_TO (statute → case facts)
    - ARGUED_BY (lawyer → case)
    - DECIDED_BY (judge → case)
  
  CRITICAL: Temporal properties on all edges
    - CITES {year: 1987, still_valid: True}
    - OVERRULED_BY {year: 2019} → invalidates previous ruling
  
QUERY EXAMPLES:
  "Find all cases that cite Brown v. Board and have been
   affirmed by the Supreme Court in the last 10 years"
   
  → MATCH (c1:Case {name: 'Brown v. Board'})
       <-[:CITES]-(c2:Case)
       -[:AFFIRMED_BY]->(sc:Case {court: 'Supreme Court'})
     WHERE sc.year >= 2014
     RETURN c2.name, sc.name, sc.year
  
CHALLENGES:
  - Case citations form a massive DAG (directed acyclic graph)
  - Need temporal reasoning on edge properties
  - Overruled cases must be flagged in traversal
  - Access control: some cases are sealed/confidential

INFRASTRUCTURE:
  - Neo4j Enterprise (ACID for legal accuracy requirements)
  - Full-text index on case text for BM25 integration
  - 12-node Neo4j cluster for read replicas
  - Separate Neo4j instance per client (data isolation)
```
